people/rosemary-radford-ruether/summary: American Catholic feminist theologian whose Sexism and God-Talk (1983) proposed that whatever denies or diminishes the full humanity of women is not redemptive. She also wrote pioneering work on ecofeminism and on Christian anti-Judaism.
people/delores-williams/summary: African American Presbyterian theologian at Union Theological Seminary whose Sisters in the Wilderness (1993) founded womanist theology on the figure of Hagar, the experience of Black women’s survival and a critique of surrogacy in atonement theory.
people/mercy-amba-oduyoye/summary: Ghanaian Methodist theologian, a deputy general secretary of the World Council of Churches, who founded the Circle of Concerned African Women Theologians in 1989 and is regarded as the mother of African women’s theology.
people/john-mbiti/summary: Kenyan Anglican priest and scholar whose African Religions and Philosophy (1969) and Concepts of God in Africa (1970) argued that Africans already knew God before missionaries arrived, making African traditional religion a preparation for the gospel. He also translated the New Testament into Kamba.
people/kosuke-koyama/summary: Japanese theologian, a missionary teacher in Thailand, whose Waterbuffalo Theology (1974) argued that theology must begin with the concrete questions of Asian farmers rather than the categories of Western systems, and whose Three Mile an Hour God (1979) spoke of the slow, patient love of God.
people/kosuke-koyama/keyIdeas/1: Theology from below in Asian cultures
people/c-s-song/summary: Taiwanese Presbyterian theologian (Pacific School of Religion) whose The Compassionate God (1982) and Theology from the Womb of Asia (1986) used Asian stories, folk tales and suffering as sources for a "transpositional" theology.
people/c-s-song/keyIdeas/1: Transposition of the gospel into Asia
people/ahn-byung-mu/summary: Korean New Testament scholar, imprisoned under the military dictatorship in the 1970s, who developed minjung theology: the minjung (the oppressed common people) are the ochlos crowd of Mark’s Gospel and the subject of history, with whom Jesus identified.
people/ahn-byung-mu/keyIdeas/0: Minjung as the ochlos of Mark
people/amos-yong/summary: Malaysian-born Assemblies of God theologian (Regent University, then Fuller) whose The Spirit Poured Out on All Flesh (2005) argued for a "pneumatological imagination" that lets Pentecostal experience of the Spirit shape a global, many-tongued theology, including of other religions and science.
people/amos-yong/keyIdeas/2: Pentecostal engagement with religions and science
people/leo-xiii/summary: Pope 1878-1903. His encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879) made the philosophy of Thomas Aquinas the norm of Catholic seminary teaching, and Rerum Novarum (1891) founded modern Catholic social teaching.
people/carl-f-h-henry/summary: American Baptist theologian, founding editor of Christianity Today (1956), whose Uneasy Conscience of Modern Fundamentalism (1947) called separatist fundamentalists to cultural and social engagement and whose six-volume God, Revelation and Authority (1976-83) defended propositional revelation.
people/theodotus-of-byzantium/summary: A learned leather-merchant from Byzantium who taught at Rome that Jesus was a man on whom the Spirit (Christ) descended at baptism; excommunicated by Bishop Victor of Rome c. 190. The founder of dynamic monarchianism.
people/theodotus-of-byzantium/keyIdeas/0: Jesus a mere man empowered at baptism
people/noetus-of-smyrna/summary: Teacher at Smyrna who taught that the Father himself was born, suffered and died — one God called Father or Son according to circumstance. Condemned by the presbyters of Smyrna; refuted in Hippolytus' Against Noetus.
people/praxeas/summary: A confessor from Asia who brought modalist teaching to Rome and opposed the Montanists. Known only through Tertullian's Against Praxeas; some scholars think the name is a pseudonym for a known figure.
people/eunomius-of-cyzicus/summary: Leading Anomoean (Heteroousian) theologian, disciple of Aetius and briefly bishop of Cyzicus. He argued that ‘unbegotten’ defines God's essence, so the begotten Son is unlike the Father in essence, and that God's essence is knowable. Refuted by Basil and Gregory of Nyssa.
people/eunomius-of-cyzicus/keyIdeas/1: The Son unlike the Father in essence
people/ulfilas/summary: ‘Apostle of the Goths’, consecrated bishop c. 341 by Eusebius of Nicomedia. He created the Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible into Gothic. A Homoian, he transmitted a non-Nicene Christianity to the Gothic peoples.
people/basil-of-ancyra/summary: Bishop of Ancyra and leader of the Homoiousian party; at the Synod of Ancyra (358) he argued that the Son is ‘like in essence’ to the Father, opposing both Arians and perceived Sabellians.
people/michael-servetus/summary: Spanish physician and polymath who described pulmonary circulation and wrote On the Errors of the Trinity (1531) and The Restoration of Christianity (1553). Condemned by Catholic authorities, he escaped to Geneva, where he was tried and burned with Calvin's support in October 1553 — a key case in debates over toleration.
people/michael-servetus/keyIdeas/0: Rejection of the Trinity of persons
people/michael-servetus/keyIdeas/1: Christ as the Son of the eternal God, not the eternal Son
people/faustus-socinus/summary: Italian theologian who settled in Poland (1579) and became the leading thinker of the Minor Reformed Church (Polish Brethren). Socinianism denied the Trinity, the pre-existence of Christ and penal satisfaction; its Racovian Catechism appeared in 1605.
people/francis-david/summary: Transylvanian reformer who moved from Catholicism through Lutheranism and Calvinism to Unitarianism, founding the Unitarian Church of Transylvania; court preacher to King John Sigismund, whose Edict of Torda (1568) granted religious freedom. He died in prison after opposing the invocation of Christ.
people/william-ellery-channing/summary: Boston Congregationalist minister whose 1819 Baltimore ordination sermon ‘Unitarian Christianity’ became the manifesto of American Unitarianism; an advocate of human dignity, moral religion and, later, abolition.
people/frank-ewart/summary: Australian-born Pentecostal minister in Los Angeles who, after the 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting, formulated Oneness theology and in 1914 began rebaptising believers in Jesus' name. His The Phenomenon of Pentecost (1947) is an early movement history.
people/clark-pinnock/summary: Canadian evangelical theologian who moved from Calvinism to Arminianism and then to open theism; lead author of The Openness of God (1994) and Most Moved Mover (2001).
people/alfred-north-whitehead/summary: English mathematician (co-author of Principia Mathematica) and Harvard philosopher whose process metaphysics (Process and Reality, 1929) became the basis of process theology.
people/alfred-north-whitehead/keyIdeas/2: God as the lure of creative advance
people/charles-hartshorne/summary: American philosopher who developed Whitehead's ideas into ‘neoclassical theism’ and panentheism, and revived the ontological argument in modal form.
people/john-b-cobb/summary: American Methodist theologian, born in Japan to missionary parents, the leading exponent of Christian process theology at Claremont; a pioneer of ecological theology and Buddhist–Christian dialogue.
people/john-zizioulas/summary: Greek Orthodox theologian and metropolitan whose Being as Communion (1985) argued that personhood and communion, grounded in the Father as cause, are ontologically primary — influential in ecumenical ecclesiology and social Trinitarianism.
people/hippolytus-of-rome/summary: Roman theologian, author of the Refutation of All Heresies and commentaries, who opposed Bishop Callistus and was exiled to Sardinia with Pope Pontian, where both died (c.235). The church order called the Apostolic Tradition, with an early eucharistic prayer and baptismal rite, has traditionally been ascribed to him, though many scholars now see it as a composite, layered document.
people/egeria/summary: Pilgrim woman, probably from Gallaecia (north-west Spain) or southern Gaul, whose letter-diary of a journey to the Holy Land (c.381–384) describes in detail the Jerusalem liturgy: daily offices, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week and Easter. It is a key witness to the formation of the liturgical year.
people/egeria/keyIdeas/0: Holy Week processions at the holy places
people/saint-yared/summary: Ethiopian church musician of Aksum, venerated as the creator of zema, the sacred chant of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and of its three modes (geʿez, ezel, araray), with the hymn collection Deggua. His life is known mainly from later hagiography.
people/saint-yared/keyIdeas/2: Liturgical music with drums and sistra
people/pius-v/summary: Dominican inquisitor turned pope who implemented the Council of Trent: he published the Roman Catechism (1566), the reformed Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (1570), imposing it on the Latin Church except where a rite older than 200 years existed. He excommunicated Elizabeth I (1570) and organised the Holy League that won at Lepanto (1571).
people/robert-barclay/summary: Scottish Quaker whose Apology for the True Christian Divinity (Latin 1676; English 1678) became the classic systematic defence of Quaker belief, including the inward light, silent worship and the rejection of outward sacraments and a paid ministry.
